title: The Opium War Wasn't Fought for Opium, It Was Fought for Tea
dek: Britain bought Chinese tea but had nothing China would buy, and China took only silver, draining the world's supply; what Britain finally picked up was Indian opium. The driver behind the 1839 war was not opium — it was tea.
why: Yangwen lays out a hard silver–opium–tea chain, and the Industrial Revolution section is counterintuitive too; but the comedy interludes eat up a fair amount of time, so the information density is middling.
who: Anyone who wants to understand the silver–opium–tea economic chain behind the Opium War; listeners interested in Chinese trade history who can tolerate a comedy host's banter.
skip: The opening guest pleasantries and the two minutes where Hugh talks about his own family tree can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: What's in a British tea bag is dust and fannings
points.body: Tea is graded by wholeness into four levels: leaf, broken leaf, fannings, dust — the last two being the siftings left over. Yangwen says the British market drinks mainly these two grades, packed into tea bags; China drinks whole leaves, with attention to leaf shape, body, and a complete ritual. Her words were that China doesn't drink dust, only leaves. Hugh jokes that dust sounds like a country singer, and Greg admits the British really are drinking fannings. Yangwen came to Britain in 1996 and still doesn't understand why milk and sugar go into tea — once added, by her standard it is ‘no longer tea’.

points.h: The Mongols wanted tea, the Central Plains wanted horses
points.body: Yangwen says tea defined China's premodern relations with Mongolia and Central Asia. Nomadic peoples were not settled and needed tea, iron pots and silk, which they could only get from China; China was a rice-and-wheat farming civilisation and lacked horses. Hence the historical tea-horse exchange, trading goods at a fixed rate. Once the relationship broke down, the Mongols, lacking tea, raided south — the 1449 Tumu crisis being the example: the Ming army was surrounded by the Mongols and some fifty thousand soldiers were captured along with the emperor. Afterward the Ming closed the Great Wall for a time, but blockade was never a long-term solution, and in the end the gates had to reopen for the tea-horse trade.

points.h: The word for tea betrays the road it travelled
points.body: Tea's spread left linguistic traces. Yangwen says that in Mongolian, Russian, Turkish, Arabic and Persian, tea is called cha, while in English it is tea — the overland camel caravan routes left cha, the sea routes left tea. Greg made a rhyme of it: ‘If it travels by car, it is cha. If it goes by the sea, it is tea.’ The value of this clue is that the same product entered different civilisations through two completely different trade networks, and even its name forked. Tea reached Europe in the early 17th century, with the Portuguese and the Dutch East India Company as the earliest suppliers.

points.h: China took only silver and drained the world dry
points.body: By the late 18th century China had sucked the world's silver into its treasury. Yangwen says that from Vasco da Gama's voyage in 1497 to 1793, Europeans and Americans came to buy tea, porcelain and silk, and China took only gold and silver; over several centuries the Europeans found they had nothing the Chinese wanted. She quotes the missionary Robert Hart: the Chinese have the best food (rice), the healthiest drink (tea), the best clothing material (silk), and need nothing from Britain. In 1793 the Macartney mission asked for free trade, and the emperor's attitude was: I permit my subjects to sell you a little tea, and that is a favour. The only thing Britain had left that could break into China was Indian opium.

points.h: Stolen green tea grew into black tea in India
points.body: In 1843, to break its dependence on Chinese tea, Britain sent the botanist Robert Fortune to infiltrate China's interior and steal tea plants. He bought a fake queue, wore a hat to cover his unshaved forehead, and travelled up into the mountains, digging up whole tea plants and shipping them back to Assam in India. Yangwen points out an irony: what he mainly stole was green tea from the southeast coast, and grown in Assam's stronger sunlight and richer soil it turned into black tea — the raw material now taken as the archetypal British black tea is in fact a Chinese green tea variety. Fortune himself did not get rich from it; Yangwen says he did not die wealthy.

points.h: The Industrial Revolution was pushed along by tea and sugar
points.body: Some economic historians have argued that the Industrial Revolution was driven by tea. Yangwen says caffeine plus the sugar in tea let the working class refuel at half past ten in the morning and half past three in the afternoon, working longer and producing more; Sydney Mintz's Sweetness and Power is the representative statement of this argument. The same logic explains why tea replaced small beer in the mid-18th century as the middle class's breakfast drink of choice. By 1923, 53% of the world's tea supply was being drunk in Britain.

points.h: Britain's tea today comes mainly from Kenya
points.body: Tea cultivation moved with the colonial map. The seedlings stolen out of China first took root in Assam in India, and in 1885 India exported 35,000 tons of tea a year, which Greg converts into 7,000 African elephants. In 1903 Britain opened plantations in Kenya, and Yangwen says Kenya is today Britain's main source of tea. She also notes that Chinese tea bought today at places like Fortnum Mason has mostly been systematically machine-cut, so the leaf shape can't be seen, and what you drink is not the kind of tea she recognises.

points.h: The tea bag cost the British tea's ritual
points.body: In the nuance window Yangwen offers a prediction: tea will revive. The reason is the environmental movement — people should eat natural things and drink natural things, and tea is a plant to begin with, like a vegetable, good for health and the environment; on the other hand, the modernisation of the tea bag makes her feel tea has lost its ritual, and perhaps its nutrition too. Greg steers the topic to the China–Britain difference: in Chinese tea drinking, the waiting itself is the ritual; the British put more emphasis on the time after the tea is brewed, chatting with people. Hugh admits he has never experienced so-called ‘slow tea’.

quotes.text: But in China, we don't drink dust. We drink leaves.
The Mongols wanted tea. We want their horse.
by the late 18th century, China had sucked in all the world's supply of silver. And China isn't buying anything from Britain.
So the opium war is a tea war. Yes, for tea.
It's Britain's desperation for silver in order to buy more tea from China that make them resort to grow opium in India and sell them to China.
the tea that he stole from China were largely green tea because they're from southeastern China. And when they harvested the tea in Assam, it became black tea.
there is an economic historian who made the case that the Industrial Revolution is powered by tea.
